## Overview

We will cover:

::: {.incremental}

* Models of multimodality using Gaussian mixtures
* Fitting model-based clustering
* Diagnostics for the model fit
* Self-organising maps and dimension reduction

:::

## Model-based clustering {.transition-slide .center}

## From algorithm to models 

::: {.incremental}

+ Last week we saw two clustering algorithms - $k$-means and hierarchical
+ These were recipes for clustering observations rather than models that explain  the data
+ Similar to how k-nearest neighbours was a recipe for supervised learning prediction...
+ ... and Logistic regression or LDA where models



:::

## Remembering LDA

::: {.incremental}

+ In supervised classification $y_i\in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ and $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$
+ LDA assumed the distribution of the features for each **known** class was multivariate normal with [class specific]{.monash-blue2} mean $\mu_k$ and [pooled]{.monash-blue2} covariance $\Sigma$
+ i.e. for $i$ with $y_i = k$ $x_i \sim f_k(\cdot; \mu_k, \Sigma)$ with 
$$
f_k(x; \mu_k, \Sigma) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp\{-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu_k)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu_k)\}
$$
+ used Bayes rule to produce a classification probability $P(y_i = k)$
+ Estimated $\mu_k$ and $\Sigma$ via maximum likelihood (class wise column means and pooled covariances) 
+ QDA relaxed equal variance and estimated [class specific]{.monash-blue2} covariance $\Sigma_k$

:::

## Mixtures and Clusters

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggscatmat(c7[,1:3], alpha=0.2)

```

## Overview

Model-based clustering makes the same assumption about the distribution of the features, except it doesn't know the class labels, primarily

::: {.incremental}

- Assumes the data in each **unknown** cluster is a sample from a Gaussian distribution
- Results in a Gaussian Mixture Model to account for the cluster labels being **unknown**
- Requires the assumption that clusters have an elliptical shape
- [The shape is determined by the variance-covariance of the clusters]{.monash-blue2}
- [A variety of models is available using different constraints on the variance-covariance]{.monash-blue2}

:::


## The model


Model assumes that the distribution of the observed data has density

$$f(x_i; \{\pi_k, \mu_k, \Sigma_k\}_{k=1}^K) = \sum_{k=1}^K\pi_kf_k(x_i; \mu_k, \Sigma_k)$$

where $f_k$ is usually a multivariate normal distribution.


::: {.fragment}

The parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood, and choice between models is made using BIC. 

:::

::: {.fragment}

$\pi_k\in(0, 1)$ with $\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k = 1$ allows us to estimate the proportion of observations in each cluster and account for unbalanced clusters

:::

## Parametrisation of the var-cov matrices [(1/2)]{.smallest}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="font-size: 80%;"}

The covariance matrix $\Sigma_k$ has $d(d+1)/2$ parameters (i.e. for $d = 10$, has 55 parameters per cluster, for $d = 50$, has 1225 parameters per cluster)

::: {.fragment}

Constraints applied on cluster variance-covariance:

$$
\Sigma_k = \lambda_kD_kA_kD_k^\top
$$

:::

::: {.incremental}

- [volume ($\lambda_k\in\mathbb{R}$)]{.monash-blue2}: size of the cluster, i.e. one cluster could be half the size of another
- [shape ($A_k \in diag(d)$)]{.monash-blue2}: difference variances in each dimension
- [orientation ($D_k \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$)]{.monash-blue2}: aligned with axes (low covariance) or not (high covariance)

:::

<br>

::: {.incremental}

- $\Sigma_k = \lambda I$ for all $k$ is model 1, EII
- $\Sigma_k = \lambda DAD^\top$ for all $k$ is model 7, EEE
- $\Sigma_k = \lambda D_kAD_k^\top$ is model 11, EEV

:::

:::
::: {.column style="font-size: 70%;" .fragment}

|Model|Family|Volume|Shape|Orientation|Identifier|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|1|Spherical|Equal|Equal|NA|EII|
|2|Spherical|Variable|Equal|NA|VII|
|3|Diagonal|Equal|Equal|Axes|EEI|
|4|Diagonal|Variable|Equal|Axes|VEI|
|5|Diagonal|Equal|Variable|Axes|EVI|
|6|Diagonal|Variable|Variable|Axes|VVI|
|7|General|Equal|Equal|Equal|EEE|
|8|General|Equal|Variable|Equal|EVE|
|9|General|Variable|Equal|Equal|VEE|
|10|General|Variable|Variable|Equal|VVE|
|11|General|Equal|Equal|Variable|EEV|
|12|General|Variable|Equal|Variable|VEV|
|13|General|Equal|Variable|Variable|EVV|
|14|General|Variable|Variable|Variable|VVV|
:::
::::

## Parametrisation of the var-cov matrices [(2/2)]{.smallest}

<center>
<img src="https://bradleyboehmke.github.io/HOML/20-model-clustering_files/figure-html/visualize-different-covariance-models-1.png" width="100%">
</center>

[Source: [Boehmke (2020) Hands-on machine learning](https://bradleyboehmke.github.io/HOML/model-clustering.html)]{.smallest}

## Reduction in the number of parameters to estimate

:::: {.columns }
::: {.column style="font-size: 90%;"}

$$
\Sigma_k = \lambda_kD_kA_kD_k^\top
$$

::: {.incremental}

+ VVV estimates a full covariance matrix $\Sigma_k$ for each cluster, the covariance matrix has $d(d+1)/2$ parameters and so we have [$K\times d(d+1)/2$ parameters]{.monash-orange}
+ EII estimates $\Sigma_k = \lambda I$ for all $k$ and so only has [$1$ parameter]{.monash-orange2}
+ EEE estimates a full covariance matrix $\Sigma$ but fixes this across clusters i.e. $\Sigma_k = \Sigma$ for all $k$ so has  [$d(d+1)/2$ parameters]{.monash-orange2}


:::

:::
::: {.column .fragment style="font-size: 90%;"}

**NOT EXAMENABLE**

::: {.incremental}

+  EVE estimates $\Sigma_k = \lambda DA_kD^\top$ so we have
  + 1 $\lambda$ across all clusters 
  + 1 matrix $D$ across all of the clusters, which to be a valid orientation/rotation has $d(d-1)/2$ elements and 
  + An $A_k$ per cluster, $A_k$ has $(d-1)$ elements as all of the other axes width  are relative to the first axes width.    
  + In total we have [$1 + d(d-1)/2 + K(d-1)$ parameters]{.monash-orange2} 

:::

:::

::::


## Reduction in the number of parameters to estimate

:::: {.columns }
::: {.column }

$$f(x_i; \{\pi_k, \mu_k, \Sigma_k\}_{k=1}^K) = \sum_{k=1}^K\pi_kf_k(x_i; \mu_k, \Sigma_k)$$

In addition to $\Sigma_k$ we must also estimate 

::: {.incremental}

+ A $\mu_k\in\mathbb{R}^d$ for each cluster $k$ (i.e. [$K\times d$ parameters]{.monash-orange2} )
+ Cluster weights $\pi_k\in\mathbb{R}^K$, while we have $K$ clusters $\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k = 1$ so $\pi_K = 1- \sum_{k=1}^{K-1}\pi_k$ so there are only [$K-1$ parameters]{.monash-orange2} 

:::


:::
::: {.column .fragment}

<br><br><br>


**You can't estimate a model with more parameters than observations!**

::: {.fragment}

*Unless you regularise...*

:::


:::

::::


## Maximum likelihood 

::: {.incremental  style="font-size: 90%;"}

+ Once a form/constraint for the covariance matrices has been decided (more on this later)
+ We learn the parameters $\mu_k$, $\Sigma_k$, $k = 1,\ldots, K$ by maximising the likelihood
+ Remember, the likelihood is the probability under the model of the observed data
+ For the Gaussian mixture model
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{l}_n(\{\mu_k, \Sigma_k\}_{k=1}^K) &= f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n; \{\mu_k, \Sigma_k\}_{k=1}^K) \\
&= \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i; \{\mu_k, \Sigma_k\}_{k=1}^K)\\
&=  \prod_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_kf_k(x_i; \mu_k, \Sigma_k)
\end{aligned}
$$
+ The Maximum likelihood estimates are the parameter that made the observed data as likely as possible
$$
\begin{aligned}
\{\hat{\mu}_k, \hat{\Sigma}_k\}_{k=1}^K := \arg\max\mathcal{l}_n(\{\mu_k, \Sigma_k\}_{k=1}^K)
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

```{r}
ggplot(data=df, aes(x1, x2)) + geom_point() +

```

## BIC

::: {.incremental  style="font-size: 90%;"}

+ The BIC stands for Bayesian Information Criteria
+ For any variance/covariance constraints we use Maximum Likelihood to estimate the parameters $\hat{\mu}_k, \hat{\Sigma}_k$
+ We can't use the likelihood to choose between models though, as the likelihood will always favour more complex models 
+ Information Criteria use the log-likelihood but also penalise model complexity 

:::

::: {.fragment}

$$
BIC = (\#parameters)\log(n) - 2\log(\mathcal{l}_n(\{\hat{\mu}_k, \hat{\Sigma}_k\}_{k=1}^K))
$$


:::

::: {.incremental}

+ $(\#parameters)$ counts the number of separate parameter reqired for $\{\hat{\mu}_k, \hat{\Sigma}_k\}_{k=1}^K$
+ $\{\hat{\mu}_k, \hat{\Sigma}_k\}_{k=1}^K$ are the maximum likelihood estimators
+ $n$ is the number of observations 
+ $\mathcal{l}_n$ is the likelihood of observations for given parameters 

:::

## Example: penguins [(1/2)]{.smallest}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

As well as selecting the covariace matrix constraints, BIC can be used to select the number of clusters 

::: {.fragment}

Let the model decide on the number of clusters, and parametrisation.

```{r echo=TRUE}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
p_mc <- mclustBIC(p_std[,2:5], G=2:8)
summary(p_mc)
```

::: 

::: {.fragment}

Maybe there really is another sub-species of penguin...

:::


:::
::: {.column style="font-size: 80%;"}

:::
::::

## Example: penguins [(1/2)]{.smallest}


```{r}
pmc1 <- ggmcbic(p_mc) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=1:7, labels=2:8)
ggplotly(pmc1)
```

<br>

::: {.fragment}

The model with the smallest BIC is the best. However, `mclust` negates the BIC so we look for the maximum.


:::



## Example: penguins [(1/2)]{.smallest}



```{r}
pmc2 <- ggmcbic(p_mc, top=6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=1:7, labels=2:8)
ggplotly(pmc2)

```


::: {.fragment}

Adopting a fully probabilistic modelling approach gives more satisfying results than the 'fit statistics' we had last week

:::

## Summary

::: {.incremental}

- Model-based clustering provides a nice [automated]{.monash-blue2} clustering, if the data has neatly separated clusters, even in the presence of nuisance variables.
- Non-elliptical clusters could be modeled by combining multiple ellipses.
- It is [affected by nuisance observations]{.monash-blue2}, and has a parameter `noise` to attempt to filter these.
- It may not function so well if the data hasn't got separated clusters.
- $k$-means and Wards linkage hierarchical would yield similar results to constraining the variance-covariance model to EEI (or VII, EEE).
- Having a [functional model]{.monash-blue2} for the clusters is useful.

:::

## Self-organising maps {.transition-slide .center}

## Overview

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="font-size: 100%;"}

::: {.incremental}

- A self-organizing map is a [constrained $k$-means]{.monash-blue2} algorithm
- A 1D or 2D net is stretched through the data. The knots in the net form the cluster means, and points closest to the knot are considered to belong to that cluster.
- The [net provides a low-dimensional summary]{.monash-blue2} of the clustering, nodes (and their corresponding clusters) that are close to each other being more similar than those that are further apart.

:::


:::
::: {.column style="font-size: 60%;" .fragment}

![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/TrainSOM.gif/440px-TrainSOM.gif){width=600}

[Source: wikipedia]{.smallest}
    
:::
::::

## The Algorithm 

::: {.incremental style="font-size: 90%;"}

1. Scale your data
2. Initialize the net defined by the knots (nodes $m_k, k=1, ..., K$): choose the number of nodes in the horizontal (and vertical directions for 2D), and set initial positions of these $K$ nodes (eg first two PCs) in the data space.
3. Loop over data points, $x_i, i=1, ..., n$
    i. find the closest node, $m_{k^*}$
    ii. for each node, $m_k$ in the neighborhood of $m_{k^*}$ and update it by: $m_k = m_k + \alpha h_k(x_i, m_{k^*})\cdot (x_i-m_{k^*})$, pulling it closer to $x_i$,
    
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size: 90%;"}
    
where $\alpha$ is a learning rate function that linearly shrinks from 1 to 0, or function with decreasing value as the number of iterations increases, and $h_k$ is a neighbourhood function, e.g. $h_k(x_i, m_{k^*})=exp(\frac{||x_i-m_{k^*}||}{2\alpha})^2)$ which is a bubble function (within a distance or not).

:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size: 90%;"}

Step 3 is iterated until nodes stop changing position or a stopping rule is satisfied.

:::
    


## Example: penguins [(1/2)]{.smallest}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

[kohonen](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/kohonen/index.html)

[somInit](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/aweSOM/versions/1.3/topics/somInit)

[som](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/class/html/SOM.html)

```{r}
set.seed(947)
p_grid <- kohonen::somgrid(xdim = 5, ydim = 5,
                           topo = 'rectangular')
p_init <- somInit(as.matrix(p_std[,2:5]), 5, 5)
p_som <- som(as.matrix(p_std[,2:5]), 
             rlen=2000,
             grid = p_grid,
             init = p_init)
```

::: {.fragment}

`rlen` controls the length of the optimisation. Tend to need to run it for longer than default.

:::

:::
::: {.column .fragment}

```{r}
plot(p_som, type="changes")
```

:::
::::

## Example: penguins [(2/2)]{.smallest}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="font-size: 80%;"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
p_som_df_net <- som_model(p_som)
p_som_data <- p_som_df_net$data |> 
  mutate(species = p_std$species)
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data=p_som_df_net$edges_s, 
               aes(x=x, xend=xend, y=y, 
                   yend=yend)) +
  geom_point(data=p_som_data, 
             aes(x=map1, y=map2, 
                 colour=species), 
             size=3, alpha=0.5) +
  xlab("map 1") + ylab("map 2") +
  scale_color_discrete_divergingx(
    palette="Zissou 1") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank())

# Set up data
p_som_map <- p_som_df_net$net |>
  mutate(species = "0", type="net")
p_som_data <- p_som_data |> 
  select(bl:bm, species) |>
  mutate(type="data", 
         species = as.character(species)) 
p_som_map_data <- bind_rows(p_som_map, p_som_data)
p_som_map_data$type <- factor(p_som_map_data$type,
  levels=c("net", "data"))
p_som_map_data$species <- factor(p_som_map_data$species,
  levels=c("0","Adelie","Chinstrap","Gentoo"))
p_pch <- c(46, 16)[as.numeric(p_som_map_data$type)]
p_col <- c("black", hcl.colors(3, "Zissou 1"))[as.numeric(p_som_map_data$species)]
```

From the map we can see that the clustering has effectively distinguished the species, with some confusion between Chinstrap and Adelie.

:::
::: {.column style="font-size: 80%;" .fragment}

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false
animate_xy(p_som_map_data[,1:4],
           col=p_col, 
           pch=p_pch,
           edges=as.matrix(p_som_df_net$edges), 
           edges.col = "black",
           axes="bottomleft")
```

## Example: surface [(3/3)]{.smallest}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="font-size: 80%;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 80%
c3_som_df_net <- som_model(c3_som)
c3_som_data <- c3_som_df_net$data 
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data=c3_som_df_net$edges_s, 
               aes(x=x, xend=xend, y=y, 
                   yend=yend)) +
  geom_point(data=c3_som_data, 
             aes(x=map1, y=map2), 
             size=3, alpha=0.5) +
  xlab("map 1") + ylab("map 2") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())
```

:::
::: {.column style="font-size: 80%;" .fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Set up data
c3_som_map <- c3_som_df_net$net |>
  mutate(type="net")
c3_som_data <- c3_som_data |> 
  select(x1:x10) |>
  mutate(type="data") 
c3_som_map_data <- bind_rows(c3_som_map, c3_som_data)
c3_som_map_data$type <- factor(c3_som_map_data$type,
  levels=c("net", "data"))
c3_pch <- c(19, 16)[as.numeric(c3_som_map_data$type)]
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false
animate_xy(c3_som_map_data[,1:3],
           pch=c3_pch,
           col=c3_som_map_data$type,
           edges=as.matrix(c3_som_df_net$edges), 
           edges.col = "#3B99B1",
           edges.width=2,
           axes="bottomleft")
render_gif(c3_som_map_data[,1:3],
           grand_tour(),
           display_xy(pch=c3_pch,
           col=c3_som_map_data$type,
           edges=as.matrix(c3_som_df_net$edges), 
           edges.col = "#3B99B1",
           edges.width = 3,
           axes="bottomleft"),
           width=400,
           height=400,
           frames=300,
           gif_file = "../gifs/c3_som.gif")
```

<center>
![](../gifs/c3_som.gif)
</center>

::: {.incremental}

- the net stretches into the vertices of the tetrahedron, filling the smaller tetrahedrons
- see the break so that a 2D net fits the 3D object?
- the 7 noise dimensions were ignored

:::
